What this calculator does

Most people know they need a calorie deficit to lose fat. Fewer know how big it should be or how long it will take. This tool answers both: it estimates the calories you burn each day, subtracts the deficit needed for your chosen pace and projects a finish date.

Seeing a realistic date up front helps. It turns a vague wish into a plan with a checkpoint, and it shows clearly why crash diets rarely save as much time as they promise.

How to use it

Enter your sex, age, height, current weight and goal weight, then pick the activity level that best describes a normal week. Finally choose a pace: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1 kg per week (about 0.5, 1, 1.5 or 2 lb).

The result shows your maintenance calories, your daily target, the number of weeks to your goal, the estimated date and the total deficit involved. If your target drops below a sensible floor, the calculator warns you.

The maths behind it

Maintenance calories come from the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, multiplied by your activity factor, the same approach used in the TDEE calculator.

Men: BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5

Women: BMR = 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age − 161

Daily deficit = pace (kg/week) × 7,700 kcal / 7

Target = BMR × activity factor − daily deficit

Weeks to goal = (current − goal weight) / pace

The 7,700 kcal per kilogram figure (about 3,500 per pound) is the standard approximation for the energy in body fat tissue. A pace of 0.5 kg per week therefore needs a deficit of about 550 kcal a day.

Choosing a pace

PaceDaily deficitBest for
0.25 kg (0.5 lb) / week~275 kcalLean lifters, last few kilos, keeping strength
0.5 kg (1 lb) / week~550 kcalMost people; sustainable and muscle-friendly
0.75 kg (1.5 lb) / week~825 kcalHigher body fat, strong adherence
1 kg (2 lb) / week~1,100 kcalLarger bodies only; hard to sustain

A useful rule is to lose about 0.5-1% of your body weight per week. Faster than that, especially when already lean, increases the risk of losing muscle, feeling flat in the gym and rebounding afterwards.

The calculator flags targets below 1,500 kcal for men and 1,200 kcal for women. Going lower is hard to meet nutritional needs on and should be done only with medical supervision.

Why the estimate drifts, and what to do

The projected date assumes your maintenance stays fixed. In reality it falls as you lose weight: a smaller body burns less, and your body adapts by reducing movement and, to a lesser extent, metabolic rate. This is called metabolic or adaptive thermogenesis. Kevin Hall's modelling work at the NIH showed that the simple 3,500 kcal rule overestimates long-term loss for this reason.

  • Recalculate every 5 kg (about 10 lb) lost, using your new weight.
  • Judge progress on weekly averages, not single weigh-ins. Water can move the scale 1-2 kg day to day.
  • Plateaus of one or two weeks are normal. If the weekly average has not moved for three weeks, cut a further 100-200 kcal or add daily steps.
  • Diet breaks of one to two weeks at maintenance every 8-12 weeks can make a long diet easier to stick to.

Keep protein high and keep lifting heavy. Those two habits do more than anything else to make sure the weight you lose is fat, not muscle.

A worked example

Take a 32-year-old woman, 165 cm tall, weighing 78 kg, who wants to reach 68 kg. She trains three times a week, so she picks the lightly active level (1.375).

BMR = 10 × 78 + 6.25 × 165 − 5 × 32 − 161 ≈ 1,490 kcal

Maintenance = 1,490 × 1.375 ≈ 2,050 kcal

At 0.5 kg per week her deficit is about 550 kcal, giving a daily target of roughly 1,500 kcal and a timeline of 20 weeks for 10 kg. At 1 kg per week the target would drop to about 950 kcal, well below the 1,200 kcal floor, and the calculator would warn her. A pace of 0.5 kg is the sensible choice.

After the first 5 kg she recalculates at 73 kg. Her maintenance has dropped to around 1,980 kcal, so her target becomes about 1,430 kcal to keep the same pace. Small adjustments like this, made on schedule, are what keep progress moving through the second half of a diet.

WeekExpected weightDaily target
078 kg~1,500 kcal
1073 kg~1,430 kcal (recalculated)
2068 kgMove towards new maintenance (~1,910 kcal)

Reaching the goal is not the end. Increase calories gradually over two to four weeks to the new maintenance level rather than jumping straight back to old habits. That reverse step is where many people regain the weight.

Who should not use this alone

If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, under 18, have diabetes or another medical condition, take medication that affects appetite or blood sugar, or have a history of disordered eating, talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before starting a deficit. The calculator gives estimates for healthy adults only.

Frequently asked questions

How many calories should I eat to lose 0.5 kg a week?

About 550 kcal less than your maintenance each day. For many adults that lands between 1,500 and 2,200 kcal, depending on size and activity.

Is losing 1 kg a week safe?

For people with a lot of weight to lose it can be, at least early on. For leaner people it usually means too much muscle loss and hunger. Around 0.5-1% of body weight per week is a safer guide.

Why am I not losing weight on my calorie target?

Common reasons are underestimated portions, weekend overeating, water retention and a maintenance estimate that is too high. Track carefully for three weeks, then lower your target by 100-200 kcal if needed.

Will my goal date be accurate?

Treat it as a best case. Your maintenance falls as you lose weight, so progress usually slows. Recalculate after every 5 kg to keep the estimate realistic.

What is the lowest calorie intake I should go to?

As a general rule, not below about 1,500 kcal for men or 1,200 kcal for women without medical supervision. Below that it is difficult to get enough protein, vitamins and minerals.

References

  1. Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, Hill LA, et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr. 1990.
